Confluence help

Confluence help

This guide holds Atlassian’s own documentation for Confluence Cloud, gathered on 18 August 2026. The categories are Atlassian’s own, taken from the trail printed above each article.

Confluence is used by whole teams, so its documentation covers the person writing a page and the person administering the site in the same estate. Administration material is kept under its own headings rather than left out, so a reader can skip it without losing it.

Actions that require an organization or site admin

Adjust permissions before downgrading to Confluence Free

Adjust permissions before downgrading to Confluence Free

The Free plan is for small teams of fewer than 10 people who are just getting started with Confluence. Confluence is completely open to logged-in users when you’re on the Free plan. That means everyone who can log in to your Confluence instance can view, add, and edit spaces and content.

While Confluence is open to logged-in users, anonymous access isn’t available on the Free plan. Only users who log in to your Confluence instance can access it.

To take advantage of Confluence permissions, restrictions, or anonymous access, upgrade your plan.

When you change from Standard or Premium to Free

When you change from Confluence Cloud Premium or Standard to Free, you’ll no longer be able to set permissions and restrictions. Here’s what you can expect when you change to the Free plan:

  • We’ll keep any global permissions, space permissions, and content restrictions you’ve already set. If needed, you’ll still be able to open up spaces and content to all users.
  • We’ll reset your instance’s default space permissions. When new spaces are created, all users will be able to view the spaces, add content to them, and more. (As mentioned above, we’ll keep the permissions you’ve already set on existing spaces.)
  • If your instance allowed anonymous users, they’ll no longer be able to access it. To set new permissions, you’ll need to go back to one of our paid plans.

This information also applies when you migrate from Confluence Data Center to Confluence Cloud Free. See our migration guides on how to do this.

Confluence Data Center is our only self-managed app offering, and our primary app offering outside of Confluence Cloud. We ended support of Confluence Server on February 15, 2024.

Open up a space to all users

After you switch to the Free plan, any permissions you’ve set on a space will remain in place. If needed, you can open up the space to all users. This will let anyone with access to your Confluence instance view the space, add content to it, and more.

You won’t be able to undo this action. If you need to reset the space permissions, you’ll have to go back to one of our paid plans.

  • Go to the space in Confluence Cloud.
  • Next to your space’s name in the sidebar, select More actions (•••), then Space settings.
  • Select General from the Space permissions card.
  • In the Upgrade for space permissions box, select Grant all users permissions for this space.
  • Select Grant permissions.
Open up content to all users

After you switch to the Free plan, any restrictions you’ve set on content will remain in place. If needed, you can open up content to all users. This will let anyone with access to your Confluence instance view and edit the content.

You won’t be able to undo this action. If you need to reset the content restrictions, you’ll have to go back to one of our paid plans.

  • Select the lock icon at the top of the content.
  • In the Upgrade for page restrictions box, select Remove this content’s restrictions.
  • Select Remove restrictions. If you’re a space admin, you can use the Restricted content tab to open up a content item in your space to all users by removing any restriction from the content.

This will remove all restrictions from the content. You won’t be able to undo this action. If you need to reset the content’s restrictions, you’ll have to go back to one of our paid plans.

  • Navigate to the desired space using the Spaces menu in the navigation or from the Home page.
  • Next to your space’s name in the sidebar, select More actions (•••), then Space settings.
  • Select Restricted from the Content card.
  • Select the lock icon next to the content whose restrictions you want to remove. This will remove all restrictions from the content.
  • Select Remove restrictions.

Invite guests to Confluence

Invite guests to Confluence

Not all teamwork happens inside the (sometimes virtual) walls of a single organization. Sometimes you need to partner with other companies to build integrations, work with agencies to bring marketing campaigns to life, bring in contractors and consultants to help get big projects over the line, and so on.

With single space guests, you can do all of that work without leaving Confluence.

Guests are free of charge (up to 5 guests per paid user). Total number of users (paid + guests) can’t exceed the current Confluence site user limit.

Important policy information

You may not convert current or former paid users to guests. The purpose behind the guest feature is to invite users outside of your organization.

Atlassian reserves the right to restrict your access to the feature if you’re not using it in compliance with this purpose and the guidelines outlined in Atlassian documentation. Atlassian also reserves the right to change the ratio of guests to paid users.

Who is considered a guest?

A guest is anyone outside your organization, its affiliates, subsidiaries, or related entities. Examples of guests include clients, vendors, freelancers, or external consultants.

To qualify as a guest, the user’s email domain must not match any domains associated with your organization, affiliates, or subsidiaries. Guests cannot join using an email domain that belongs to the organization’s account.

Atlassian reserves the right to restrict your access to the feature if you’re not using it in compliance with this purpose and the guidelines outlined in Atlassian documentation. Atlassian also reserves the right to change the ratio of guests to paid users.

To dive deeper into what to expect when collaborating with guests, see What can guests see and do in Confluence?

Guests are not currently supported in Confluence mobile apps. For more information, see jira.atlassian.com.

Give guests access to your Confluence site

To give guests access to your site, you need to:

  • Invite them to join your Atlassian organization.
  • Give them app access to Confluence as a guest.
  • Assign them the space they’ll be collaborating in. Guests can’t use Confluence at all without space access

See Assign space access to guests for directions on how to get guests assigned the right space access.

Note: Any guest that has app access to Confluence can access any spaces on that site that allow anonymous users.

Manage external users with added security

When bringing external people into your Confluence data, there’s always tension between the value of that collaboration and having clear and confident control over what areas of your data those external people should access.

With Atlassian’s external user security features, you can sleep well at night. These include:

  • Two-step verification
  • Periodic re-verification
  • Reviewing external users before changing security settings
  • API token access Available external user security policy settings
Invite guests and give them Confluence access

Only organization or site admins can invite guests to Confluence.

The first step in getting guests set up and collaborating on your Confluence site is to invite them to join your Atlassian organization. Next, those guests need to be given access to Confluence.

Give guests Confluence access individually

You can invite up to 10 guests at a time using this path.

  • Go to admin.atlassian.com. If you have more than one organization, select the one you want.
  • Select Directory, then Users.
  • Select Invite users.
  • Add the email addresses of the guests you want to invite. (You can invite up to 10 guests at time.)
  • Open the app role dropdown for Confluence.
  • Unselect the User role.
    • If you don’t unselect this, the user will be considered a regular paid user.
  • Select the Guest role.
  • Make sure to select the correct role for all other apps.
  • If in doubt, skip the Group membership field. It’s not required.
  • (Optional) Personalize the email invite that the guests will receive.
  • Select Invite users. This is the 1st of a 2 step process. Guests can’t access Confluence until you assign space access for them.
Give guests Confluence access via a guest group

Access management is often easier to manage (especially at scale) using groups.

To create a group, see Create groups.

To change a group into a guest group:

  • Go to admin.atlassian.com and select the Directory tab.
  • Select Groups in the side navigation.
  • Search for the group you want to make a guest group.
  • Select the group name or Show details.
  • Go to the Group app access section at the bottom.
  • Find the right Confluence site and change the app role to Guest. The group itself (as an object) won’t be added to Confluence. The system will read all members of the group and add them individually.

To invite new guests and give them Confluence access via a guest group:

  • Go to admin.atlassian.com.
  • Select Directory, then Users.
  • Select Invite users.
  • Add the email addresses of the guests you want to invite. (You can invite up to 10 guests at time.)
  • Unselect all roles for all apps.
  • Search for and select the group or groups that you want to assign the guest to.
  • (Optional) Personalize the email invite that the guests will receive.
  • Select Invite users. As long as all groups you’ve selected have the guest role assigned to them, the users you’re adding to them will be granted the guest role automatically.

Make sure all groups are assigned the guest role

If any groups you add guests to have the “User” or “App admin” role, the guests will be given regular access to Confluence and considered paid users.

Give guests full access to Confluence

If working with your guest requires deeper collaboration, you can promote them into a licensed user with full access to Confluence.

To give a guest full access:

  • Go to admin.atlassian.com.

  • Select Directory, then Users.

  • Search for the guest you want to promote.

  • Select the user’s name or •••, then Show details.

  • In App access, find the right Confluence site and open the app role dropdown.

  • Select User.

  • Unselect Guest. To give a guest group full access:

  • Go to admin.atlassian.com and select the Directory tab.

  • Select Groups in the side navigation.

  • Search for the group you want to make a guest group.

  • Select the group name or Show details.

  • Go to the Group app access section at the bottom.

  • Find the right Confluence site and change the app role to User.

Remove a guest’s access to Confluence

There are two ways to stop a guest from accessing Confluence:

  • unassign them from a space
  • remove their app access To unassign a guest from a space, see instructions in Assign space access to guests.

Without access to any space, a guest can’t access Confluence at all but will remain in the guest list. An app admin or space admin can reassign them to a space at any time.

To remove a guest from Confluence altogether:

  • Go to admin.atlassian.com.
  • Select Directory, then Users.
  • Search for the guest you want to remove app access for.
  • Select the user’s name or •••, then Show details.
  • In App access, find the right Confluence site, open the app role dropdown, and unselect the check next to Guest. This will remove the guest from the guests in Confluence Admin.

Manage your storage usage

Manage your storage usage

With Confluence, you can feel confident knowing that your files and data are safeguarded in a secure environment. Each Confluence subscription offers a different amount of storage for your team’s needs.

  • Confluence Free- 2 GB
  • Confluence Standard- 250 GB
  • Confluence Premium- Unlimited storage
Tracking your storage usage

You must be a Confluence admin to view and track your storage.

  • Go to admin.atlassian.com and select your organization(if you have more than one). You can also get to this page by switching to the Administration tab using the menu in Confluence.
  • This step is different depending on your user management settings:
    • Original: On the left nav bar, select the site’s name and URL to open the Admin for that site.
    • Centralized: Select Apps then select the site’s name and URL to open the Admin for that site.
  • Under Site settings, select Storage.
  • For each app, you’ll see the amount of storage used and the amount remaining (if it’s not unlimited). This data may not reflect your most current storage usage, since it’s updated only every 4 hours.
Managing your storage

All pages, live docs, attachments, files, and comments take up storage. We recommend removing the biggest attachments and files to help free up some storage space. The quickest way to clear storage would be to delete pages or live docs with attachments.

Removing attachments

Archiving content that contain attachments in Confluence will not free up any storage. This is because Confluence keeps files to make historical data available to you. To free storage, we recommend deleting the content altogether.

Regarding attachments, you’ll need to delete them from archived pages and live docs or delete archived page or live docs completely. Once again, this is because Confluence stores all attachments for version history purposes.

What happens if I exceed my storage limit?

When you reach storage limits for your Confluence plan, you’ll either need to upgrade to a higher plan or remove content that is taking up storage. If you don’t take action within the dedicated time frame, your team will not be able to edit or create spaces, pages, live pages, whiteboards, and content within your Confluence site.

Removing users and downgrading to Confluence Free

Removing users and downgrading to Confluence Free

When you downgrade from our Premium or Standard to a Free plan, you’ll lose access to certain features including analytics, user permissions, guest collaboration, and more. View our pricing page for a full list of Premium and Standard features.

Prerequisites

You must be a Confluence admin to make changes to your plan selection.

If you have more than 10 users, you won’t be able to switch to our Free plan. This is because our Free plan is limited to a maximum of 10 users per site. Therefore, you’ll need to remove any additional users before you can downgrade.

Removing Confluence users

To remove users from your Confluence site:

  • Go to admin.atlassian.com.
  • On the Overview page, select More actions (…) next to Confluence.
  • From the dropdown menu, select Manage users.
  • Locate the user you wish to remove and select More actions (…) next to their name.
  • From the dropdown menu, select Suspend. This action removes the user from your site. Repeat until you have 10 or fewer users.

How to downgrade

To downgrade and change your plan selection:

  • Go to admin.atlassian.com and select the billing tab.
  • Under Products and Apps, look for Confluence and select Manage.
  • Under Active Subscriptions, find your Confluence Premium subscription.
  • Select Change and pick Free.
  • Lastly, you’ll need to acknowledge the terms and conditions before you select Confirm plan change to save your changes.

What happens to my permissions when I downgrade?

When you downgrade, you’ll still have access to all of your content in Confluence. Content access will not change. As an admin, you can still grant access to restricted content (content that has been set to private), but you won’t be able to create content and set it as private or restrict access. Learn more about Confluence permissions.

What happens when an account is deactivated vs. deleted?

What happens when an account is deactivated vs. deleted?

Organization admins can deactivate or delete accounts they manage for users who no longer need to use Atlassian account services. When an account is deactivated or deleted, the user will immediately lose access to Confluence and all other Atlassian account services, and we’ll stop billing for their account.

  • If an organization admin deactivates a user’s account, the user’s personal data will remain in Atlassian account services, and the admin can reactivate their account at any time.
  • If an organization admin deletes a user’s account, we’ll delete the user’s personal data from Atlassian account services, and no one will be able to reactivate their account. An organization admin can delete a previously deactivated account if they decide to later.
What’s deleted?

When you delete a user’s account, we’ll permanently delete their personal data from all Atlassian account services. Their name will be replaced by Former user throughout Confluence, and their Confluence personal space will be archived.

We won’t delete:

  • Pages, live docs, blog posts, whiteboards, databases, comments, or files. To manually delete the content they’ve created, users will need to follow the instructions in Delete, restore, or content.
  • Personal data in user-generated content. If the user’s personal data, such as their name, email address, or phone number, appears in the text of a Confluence Cloud page or live doc, it will remain on Confluence Cloud until the content or the site is deleted. To delete personal data from pages, live docs, whiteboards, blog posts, or comments, the user will need to find the content using global search, then edit it to manually remove their data. Once an account has been deleted, both the account and the personal data in it are gone forever.
How they’ll appear

This is what the deleted user will look like to other Confluence users once their account is deleted:

Advanced tools and workflows in whiteboards

Export or import your whiteboard

Export or import your whiteboard

Whiteboards aren’t available in Atlassian Government environments.

Exporting your whiteboard allows you to save your work in various file formats for easy sharing and documentation. Here are the available export options and the steps to export your whiteboard.

Export your whiteboard
  • Open the more menu (...) from the top of the whiteboard.
  • Select Export.
  • Select a file type and export area.
  • Select Export. The file for the exported whiteboard will begin downloading to your device.
Export options
  • File type: PDF, PNG, JPG
  • Export area:
    • Entire board: Exports the entire whiteboard, capturing all content within it.
    • Selected area: This option allows you to export specific parts of the whiteboard. Make sure some items on the board are selected to use this option.
Import your whiteboard
  • Navigate to the whiteboard where you wish to import the exported whiteboard. You can use an existing whiteboard or start a new one.
  • You can import your content in two ways:
    • Drag your image or file into your whiteboard.
    • On the toolbar, select the More action menu ( ), select Whiteboard import, navigate to your file, and select it.
  • Select your content type.
  • The import process will complete.
  • Note: The whiteboard imported is non-editable.

Import to whiteboards from Miro, Mural, and Figjam

Import to whiteboards from Miro, Mural, and Figjam

Whiteboards aren’t available in Atlassian Government environments.

Bring your content from other tools to Confluence whiteboards and collaborate seamlessly with your team. Whiteboards support import of boards from Miro, Mural, and Figjam.

Export from Miro

Need to export and import multiple boards? Organizations on a Miro Enterprise plan can use a bulk exporter.

Import your whiteboards from Miro into Confluence to unlock features like smart connectors, smart sections, real-time editing, and experience brainstorming and collaboration like never before. Plus, keep everything organized with your whiteboards conveniently stored alongside your other Confluence content.

Export your Miro board
  • In Miro, open the board you wish to export.
  • Open the export menu in the top-left corner of the board, then select Save as image.
  • Select the area of the board that you’d like to export.
  • Select the Vector option.
  • Click the Export button.
  • Continue to Import to whiteboards below. For more information on exporting Miro boards, see the Miro support documentation.

You must use Save as image to import editable elements to your Confluence whiteboard.

Export from Mural

Need to import multiple Mural boards? Use our bulk importer.

Import whiteboards from Mural into Confluence to unlock features such as smart connectors, smart sections, real-time editing, and experience brainstorming. Plus, you can keep everything organized with your whiteboards conveniently stored alongside your other Confluence content.

Export your Mural board
  • In Mural, open the board you wish to export.
  • Open the export menu in the top-left corner of the board, then select Download mural, or right-click on your board’s background and select Download.
  • Select the PDF Format and the selection of content you would like to export (All content, Selection, or Outline),
  • Select Download. Select a location to save your file. For more information on exporting Mural boards, see the Mural support documentation.

You must use Save as PDF. This will let you import editable elements to your Confluence whiteboard.

Export from Figjam

Import your whiteboards from Figjam into Confluence to unlock features like smart connectors, smart sections, real-time editing, and experience brainstorming and collaboration like never before. Plus, keep everything organized with your whiteboards conveniently stored alongside your other Confluence content.

Export your Figjam board
  • In Figjam, open the board you wish to export.
  • Select the Main menu icon in the top-left corner, then select File > Export As.
  • In the Export dialog, select from PNG, JPG, or PDF.
  • If exporting as PNG or JPG, select a Background option (Transparent, Solid, or Grid).
  • For the Export area, you can select the entire board, or Selection only.
  • Select the Export button.
  • Select a location to save the file.
  • Continue to Import to whiteboards below. For more information on exporting Figjam boards, see the Figma support documentation.
Import to whiteboards
  • Navigate to the whiteboard where you wish to import the image or PDF. You can use an existing whiteboard or start a new one.
  • You can import your content in two ways:
    • Drag your image or file into your whiteboard.
    • On the toolbar, select the More menu ( … ), select Whiteboard import, navigate to your file, and select it.
  • Select your content type.
  • The import process will complete.
When should I recreate my content in Confluence whiteboards vs. uploading a static image?

For projects that are still in progress and continue to be iterated on, we recommend importing as an image and recreating the areas that require additional editing and changes.

For projects that are completed, but may need to be referenced in the future, we recommend importing as an image. The content will then live in Confluence whiteboards as the new source of record.

Limitations

Some limitations and differences between your external tools and Confluence whiteboard will occur.

  • Importing comments from other tools is not supported, but you can comment on Confluence whiteboards.
  • Colors will be mapped to the closest Confluence whiteboards colors.
  • Connectors will not import, but they can be recreated in Confluence whiteboards.
  • Rotated elements will import unrotated.
  • Shapes supported in whiteboards will import as shapes. Shapes that are not supported will import as images.
  • Locked elements will not remain locked when imported, but you can manually lock them in Confluence whiteboards.
  • Talk tracks are not supported in whiteboards.
  • Whiteboards have a 10,000-element limit.
  • Importing may take longer than a minute for boards with many elements, large images, or a lot of content.

Integrate whiteboards into your Atlassian workflow

Integrate whiteboards into your Atlassian workflow

Whiteboards aren’t available in Atlassian Government environments.

Embed your whiteboard in other products, move ideas to Jira, and create or import Jira work items.

Embed your entire whiteboard into Jira, Confluence, and Trello

Easily embed ideas and add visualization to your workflows by embedding a whiteboard Smart Link into project posters, product roadmaps, kanban boards, and more.

Move ideas from your whiteboard into Jira work items and other Confluence content items

If you’re not looking to showcase your entire whiteboard somewhere else, simply take the ideas with you to your other apps. Get things happening after a retro by copying text, sticky notes, or shapes into a Confluence page or a Jira work item description.

  • Select the sticky notes, text boxes, or shapes you want to copy.
  • Use Cmd + c / Ctrl + c.
  • Go to any plain text editor where you want this content to be.
  • Use Cmd + v / Ctrl + v.
Import Jira work items onto a whiteboard

You can import Jira work items onto a whiteboard in two ways: Copy and paste the link to a Jira work item onto your whiteboard, or use the Jira work item import dialog. This works for the cloud versions of Jira, Jira Service Management, and Jira App Discovery.

The Jira work item import dialog lets you search for and insert single or multiple Jira work items into your whiteboard. You can ask Rovo to search for you, use a simple plain text search, or run a more advanced Jira Query Language (JQL) search to find work items. Learn more about searching with JQL

Use the drop-down to select between Jira sites and Jira spaces (formerly projects).

Use Rovo to search

Write a short prompt describing what you’re looking for.

Use plain text search in the dialog:
  • Enter your query into the search field.
  • Select as many work items from the list as you would like to import.
  • Select Import work items.
Use JQL search in the dialog:
  • Select JQL near the search bar.
  • Enter your JQL query in the search field.
  • Select as many work items from the list as you would like to import.
  • Select Import work items.
Create Jira work items from your whiteboard

Quickly turn sticky notes or shapes into single or multiple Jira work items - be it in Jira, Jira Service Management, or Jira App Discovery. This will help take ideas in a whiteboard and turn them into actionable work items in Jira.

To turn a sticky or shape into a Jira work item:

  • Select a sticky or shape with text inside it.
  • Select + Create a Jira work item from the floating toolbar.
  • Select a site, space, and work type from the options in the picker. Note that the required input fields will update depending on the space and work item you select.
  • Fill in all required fields, then select Create.

Link Jira work items from your whiteboard

Link Jira work items from your whiteboard

Whiteboards aren’t available in Atlassian Government environments.

Adding connector lines between Jira work items on the whiteboard helps you visualize the relationships, hierarchies, and dependencies between different pieces of work. These lines can then be turned into work item links in Jira. Any link between two Jira items created in a whiteboard will update the “Linked issues” field in Jira.

Whiteboards only support linking issues from Jira Cloud sites.

Link Jira issues from your whiteboard
  • Add Jira issues to your whiteboard. You can do this by:
    • importing Jira issues
    • copy and paste the link to a Jira issue
    • turning sticky notes into single or multiple Jira issues
  • Connect the Jira issues with a line.
  • Select the line.
  • Select the Link issues button on the floating toolbar.
  • From the menu that appears, choose the type of link (for example, “blocked by”).
  • To change the direction of the link, select the Reverse icon that appears to the right of the menu.
  • Select Link.
  • The line now has a label that shows the link you created in Jira.
Edit links in Jira from your whiteboard

You can edit the links you’ve created from the whiteboard (for example, changing “blocks” to “depends on”). Editing links from the whiteboard will update the link in Jira.

To edit a link:

  • Select the line between the two Jira issues.
  • Select the Edit link button from the floating toolbar.
  • From the menu that appears, change the type of link.
  • To change the direction of the link, select the Reverse icon that appears to the right of the menu.
  • Select Update.
  • The line label now shows the link you updated in Jira.
Remove links in Jira from your whiteboard

You can remove links between Jira issues by unlinking them. Unlinking issues from the whiteboard will also remove the link in Jira.

To remove a link:

  • Select the line between the two Jira issues.
  • Select the Edit link button from the floating toolbar.
  • Select the Unlink icon that appears to the right of the menu.
  • Select Unlink.
  • The line label is now removed, and the link has been removed in Jira. You can also remove links from inside Jira. Links removed from inside Jira will also be removed from the whiteboard. Learn more about removing links from Jira.
Deleting and disconnecting lines

Deleting or disconnecting a line doesn’t remove links between issues in Jira.

Rovo in Confluence whiteboards

Rovo in Confluence whiteboards

Whiteboards aren’t available in Atlassian Government environments.

Rovo acts as a virtual teammate in your Confluence whiteboards, helping you bridge the gap between unstructured brainstorming and structured documentation. Use Rovo to generate ideas, create diagrams, and organize your content to move projects forward faster.

Rovo respects your existing permissions and can reference context from other Atlassian apps, like Jira, to provide more relevant suggestions.

Before you begin

To use Rovo in whiteboards, an org admin must activate Rovo for your site.

The Rovo panel

Use the Rovo panel to interact with AI and manage your whiteboard content. Located at the bottom-right of your whiteboard, the Rovo button opens the Rovo panel.

  • Quick actions: At the top of the panel, you can select options such as Generate diagram, Explore ideas, Summarize what I’m looking at, What should I work on next?, and Identify any key action items or decisions captured in this whiteboard. These options may shift based on Rovo’s analysis of your whiteboard.
  • Context: Shows the current focus of Rovo – your whiteboard.
  • Input box: Use this to “Ask, @mention, or / for actions” to give Rovo specific instructions.
  • Connected apps: At the bottom of the panel, you can find icons for Jira, Calendar, Slack, and Trello to pull in external context.
  • Auto: Select this option to change how Rovo answers.
Ways to use Rovo in whiteboards

Rovo helps teams move from ideation to execution by grounding AI suggestions in your organization’s unique knowledge.

Brainstorming and idea generation

Rovo helps teams overcome the “blank canvas” problem by generating initial content based on organizational knowledge.

  • Kickstart sessions: Use a prompt like “Create a whiteboard template for user research” to have Rovo generate relevant sticky notes based on your team’s previous research in Confluence.
  • Contextual brainstorming: Link a Product Requirements Document (PRD) to your prompt, and Rovo will incorporate that specific context into the generated ideas.
Sprint and quarterly planning

Rovo can programmatically structure planning boards by querying your project data.

  • Automated board setup: Ask Rovo to “Create a planning whiteboard for Project Atlas with our current epics arranged by priority.” Rovo will query Jira and arrange epics into priority swimlanes with assignee labels and status colors already applied.
  • Brainstorm-to-action: After a planning session, you can bulk-convert sticky notes into Jira issues. The sticky notes are replaced by live Jira issues (displayed as cards) linked directly to Jira.
Visualizing complex systems

Rovo can turn plain text descriptions into structured visual diagrams.

  • Architecture diagrams: Prompt Rovo to “Create an AWS diagram for an event-driven architecture” to generate a technical flowchart.
  • Process mapping: Use prompts like “Plot an email drip campaign flow” to create mind maps or flowcharts that visually organize marketing or operational processes.
Post-meeting synthesis

Rovo helps transition from a collaborative session to a formal record.

  • Retrospective conversion: After a sprint retro, ask Rovo to “Turn our retro notes from today’s Confluence page into a whiteboard.” Rovo will create a three-column board (What went well / What didn’t / Action items) and populate it with appropriately colored sticky notes.
  • Action item extraction: Use the Rovo panel to “Identify any key action items or decisions captured in this whiteboard” to ensure nothing is lost after the session ends.
Get help with sticky notes

You can use Rovo to group existing ideas or generate new ones based on what’s already on the board.

To group similar items:

  • Select two or more sticky notes on your whiteboard.

  • Select Ask Rovo in the floating toolbar.

  • Prompt Rovo to group or organize your sticky notes. To generate new ideas from a single item:

  • Select a sticky note.

  • Select Ask Rovo in the floating toolbar.

  • Prompt Rovo to add more related sticky notes.

Summarize a whiteboard

When your brainstorming session is complete, Rovo can summarize the entire board and help you transition to a structured document.

To summarize your whiteboard:

  • Select the Rovo button at the bottom-right of the screen.
  • Select Summarize what I’m looking at.
  • Select Create page to turn the summary into a new page, or select Copy summary to paste it elsewhere. The new page will contain the structured summary, allowing you to share the outcomes of your whiteboard session with the wider team.

Take bulk Jira actions with smart sections

Take bulk Jira actions with smart sections

Whiteboards aren’t available in Atlassian Government environments.

Smart sections are super-charged sections that help make your collaboration sessions more efficient. Smart sections take the effort out of making updates to Jira work items after planning sessions, helping you and your team move work forward effortlessly.

Creating a smart section

Start by adding a section to the whiteboard, by selecting the section element from the global toolbar. Once you’ve added a section to your whiteboard, select the section to trigger the element/floating toolbar.

  • Select Create action button to open the configuration panel.
  • Choose a site and space.
  • From the options in the picker, select the fields you want to use in the smart section. The configuration panel updates with fields you can edit.
  • Edit each field you want to include in the smart section.
  • Select Save.
  • Start dragging Jira work items into the section to update in real-time and have this change reflected in Jira. Note: Smart sections currently only support Jira actions, therefore only Jira work items dragged into the section will have the action applied.
Editing a smart section

To update or change an existing smart section:

  • Select the section.
  • From the floating toolbar, select the Jira integrations icon.
  • Select ‘Edit action’.
  • Make any changes to the fields.
  • Select Save.
  • Or select Clear action to remove all actions previously configured. Actions previously applied to Jira work items already in the section will still remain.
Deleting a smart section

To delete a smart section:

  • Select the section.

  • Press Delete / Backspace. Deleting a section will also delete its contents. To delete a section without deleting its contents;

  • Select everything in the section.

  • Drag it to another place on the whiteboard.

  • Select the section and press Delete / Backspace.

Undo with smart sections

Performing an ‘Undo’ after moving a work item into a section will not undo the Jira action.

Atlassian Marketplace apps

Manage your apps

Manage your apps

About apps

An app (sometimes called an add-on or plugin) is a separately installed component that provides Confluence functionality.

There are two main types of apps:

  • System apps - these are bundled with Confluence and provide core functionality.
  • User installed apps - these are usually downloaded from the Marketplace and may have been created by Atlassian or by a third party developer. For information about developing your own apps for Confluence, see Confluence Cloud developer documentation.
Find and add new apps

In Confluence Cloud terms, you buy an app by subscribing to it.

To find and try new apps in Confluence:

  • Select Apps in the navigation.
  • Select Manage your apps, which directs you to Connected apps.
  • Select Discover new apps, which directs you to the Atlassian Marketplace. Once you’re there, you can use the search and filters to find apps in Marketplace to help you get more done in Confluence. To try or subscribe to an app, click the Try it free button next to the app listing.

Some apps offer multiple editions - Standard and Advanced. The pricing and feature differences between these editions are listed under the Pricing tab on the Marketplace listing.

If you don’t terminate the trial within the trial period, a subscription for the app kicks in. Trials last for a month from the start of your next billing date. After starting a trial, you can stop it from the Administration page.

Although you can re-enable the trial within the original trial period, you can’t try it again beyond the original trial period. At that point, you can only subscribe to the app from the Manage apps page.

Manage apps

Apps are managed via Connected Apps in Administration or within the app itself. It provides a centralized experience for administering apps. To manage your apps in Connected Apps, go to admin.atlassian.com and select your organization if you have more than one. Depending on your user management experience, you can select:

  • Admin > Site settings > Connected apps

  • or Apps > Site settings > Connected apps Connected Apps allows you to:

  • Discover and install new apps from the Atlassian Marketplace

  • Install or remove apps

  • Configure app settings

  • Upgrade app editions, if applicable You need to be an Atlassian cloud site admin to access Connected Apps.

Uninstall or unsubscribe from apps

To cancel your subscription to an app, go to Settings > Atlassian Marketplace > Manage apps, select the app, and then select Uninstall.

You’ll be able to either:

  • Uninstall now to remove the app immediately (forfeiting the rest of the billing period).
  • Cancel uninstall to keep the app.
  • Keep the app until the end of the billing or trial period, then for an additional 60 days before it is automatically removed. After the app is uninstalled, the app data is retained for a limited period (30 days) before being permanently deleted. The app will no longer appear in Connected Apps or the host product once removal is complete.

Apps that use events (such as Confluence page creation) to trigger outbound webhooks can continue to send their events while the app is pending uninstallation.

To remove all data and stop outbound webhooks, uninstall the app.

View the apps audit log

The audit log displays administration activities related to apps on your Confluence Cloud instance. For example, the log displays when apps were enabled or disabled, and shows the username of the administrator who made the change.

  • Select the wheel icon () in the top-right corner to open Confluence administration.
  • Find Settings in the left-hand navigation.
  • Select Atlassian Marketplace > Manage apps.
  • Choose Audit log at the bottom-left of the page. To receive the audit log activity in an RSS feed, click the orange RSS icon on the right above the list.

Status page: Live docs + Marketplace apps

Status page: Live docs + Marketplace apps

Which Marketplace apps are supported by Live Docs?

Live Docs, a feature currently in beta, support apps that appear in:

  • The “Apps” item in the overflow menu
  • The content byline below a live doc’s title
  • The contextual menu that appears when a user highlights text
  • A banner that apps can put above Live docs
  • Macros Other locations for apps not in this list that have historically been supported by pages are not supported on live docs.

Note that some apps may not yet be fully functional as expected. Developers are also participating in testing live docs and are working on having their apps fully functional by the time they reach general availability.

App locations impacted by content layout updates

Customers with Live Docs beta enabled also received updates to the content layout in Confluence.

With this content layout update, marketplace app buttons that have historically lived in the area at the top of your page will no longer appear, both on live docs and pages. This change is meant to simplify how apps are interacted with in Confluence.

Some popular examples of apps that have buttons in this header area:

  • AURA Content Formatting Macros (Tabs Theme Miro Figma HTML)
  • Comala Publishing
  • Excel-like Tables for Confluence (Spreadsheet and Chart)
  • Handy Macros for Confluence (Status, Dropdown & Formatting)
  • Mosaic: Content Formatting Macros & Templates
  • Numbered Headings
  • Refined Sites for Confluence (Intranets, Documentation, KBs)
  • ScriptRunner for Confluence
  • Scroll Documents for Confluence
  • Source Editor for Confluence
  • Table Filter, Charts & Spreadsheets for Confluence Note that some apps that usually have buttons in the header may still be usable via other extension points that are still available in the updated layout. Apps that appear in the content byline, overflow menu, macros, and general banner extension points will still be available.

Marketplace developers have been asked to move any app buttons that currently live in the header to other extension points by April 30, 2025. That means that app buttons that usually live in the header area today will not be available on your EAP site until developers update them (either on April 30, 2025 or later if they do not make the changes on time).

Opting out of these content layout changes

We understand that apps can be critical to customer workflows, so if you would like to opt out of these content layout changes in order to maintain access to apps that live in the header area (while remaining part of the Live Docs beta), you can do so by submitting a support request.

Add a reaction to any content

Add a reaction to any content

Has someone written a good blog post, live doc, or page on Confluence? Or made a comment you agree with? Click Add a reaction to let them know.

When you react to a page, live doc, blog post, or comment, the author of the content receives a notification. If enough people add reactions to the content, it’ll appear in the Popular section of the Home Feed.

Disabling notifications from reactions

There are two ways to turn the Someone reacted to your content notifications off.

Do either of the following:

  • Open an email notification of a reaction and click Manage Notifications
  • Go to <your confluence URL>/wiki/plugins/likes/view-notifications.action A Confluence site admin can also completely disable reactions on your site.

Add people to Confluence from Google, Slack, or Microsoft

Add people to Confluence from Google, Slack, or Microsoft

Confluence is all about working together to get the best results for you and your team.

Now you can add anyone to Confluence from Google, Slack, or Microsoft (or all three). It’s quick, convenient, and secure.

Once your teammate is added, they can collaborate with you directly in Confluence.

Depending on your access settings, an admin may need to approve your request first.

Add a teammate
  • Select More and then Teams.
  • Select Add people.
  • Select Google, Slack, or Microsoft.
  • Allow Atlassian access to connect Confluence to your Google, Slack or Microsoft accounts.
  • Enter your teammate’s info and they’ll get an email inviting them to collaborate with you. You can continue to add people using their email address if you prefer.

Collaborate on Confluence content with AI agents

Collaborate on Confluence content with AI agents

Collaborate directly with Rovo agents or other AI agents by mentioning them in Confluence comments. Using artificial intelligence and machine learning, Rovo is an AI tool that is integrated into our cloud-based apps. To invoke agents that you mention in Confluence editor or comments, you’ll need to complete the following.

To get started

  • You’ll need to be a site admin to enable Rovo, AI features, or MCP agents. What are the different types of admin roles?
  • Enable Rovo and Confluence AI on your site. Manage Rovo access The quality, accuracy, and reliability of information generated by AI may vary. Find out why

When you mention an agent in a Confluence comment, you start a chat with that agent in Rovo. The agent uses the comment and page context to help with first drafts, quick summaries, and specific tasks while you keep collaborating where the work is happening.

Agents that are restricted to you won’t appear in the mention picker. If you can’t see an agent in Rovo Chat, you won’t see it when you search for agents in comments.

In Confluence, you can collaborate with agents in page comments and inline comments, and in the editor.

Set up a Rovo agent for collaboration

Have a think about which agent will best suit the task, and switch agents if your requirements change.

Once it’s set up to collaborate in Confluence, you can mention a Rovo agent by Atlassian, a Rovo agent created by someone in your site, or an agent built by a third party.

Read how to add an external MCP server from Atlassian Administration

To work with a Rovo agent in Confluence:

  • In the top left navigation, select Switch sites or apps.
  • Select Studio, then Agents.
  • Select View my agents.
  • Choose either Browse agents or Create an agent. Read how to create and edit Rovo agents and Rovo agent permissions and governance.
Mention an agent in Confluence editor

You can mention multiple agents in the editor, but can only interact with one at a time.

In the Confluence editor, you can mention agents in an action item, a paragraph or list, or in a table.

Mention an agent in an action item

When you mention an agent in an action item, Confluence assumes a specific task is required and automatically opens the Rovo Chat interface.

  • Type [] or select Action item from the toolbar.
  • Describe the task you want the agent to perform.
  • Type @ and select the agent’s name.
  • Trigger the agent by doing one of the following:
    • Stop typing for three seconds.
    • Select away from the action item.
    • Select Enter.
  • The Rovo chat will open automatically with your task text already populated as a submitted prompt.
Mention an agent in a paragraph or list

For lists, only the text from the specific line item containing the mention is sent to the chat, not the entire list.

For mentions in paragraphs or lists, the intent is often informational. Confluence provides a “nudge” so you can choose whether or not to start a task. To mention an agent in a paragraph or list:

  • Type your content in a paragraph or a bulleted/numbered list.
  • Type @ and select the agent’s name.
  • Trigger the nudge by stopping for three seconds, clicking away, or selecting Enter.
  • When the Start chatting with agent nudge appears, select it to open the chat.
  • Review the drafted prompt in the chat window, edit if necessary, and select Send.
Mention an agent in a table

If the table cell is empty, the agent will be mentioned but no prompt will be drafted.

Mentioning an agent within a table cell focuses the agent’s context specifically on the content of that cell. To mention an agent in a table:

  • Select a table cell and enter your text.
  • Type @ and select the agent’s name.
  • Trigger the nudge by stopping for three seconds, clicking away, or selecting Enter.
  • Select the Start chatting with agent nudge.
  • The chat will open with the content of that specific cell as a drafted prompt.
Mention an agent in a comment

Mentioning more than one agent in the same comment isn’t supported yet.

To invoke and interact with an agent in a comment, open the Confluence content (for example, a page, whiteboard, or live doc) you want to work on, and:

  • Start a general comment or an inline comment. Read about adding comments
  • In the comment, enter @, then start typing the name of the agent you want to invoke.
  • Choose the agent from the menu. You may see a mix of people and agents, depending on who or what you’ve recently worked with.
  • Finish typing your request as a comment, then select Add. While you’re drafting, Confluence lets you know that the agent will respond in Rovo Chat. After you publish the comment, Rovo Chat opens in the side panel with the mentioned agent selected and the conversation started.

The agent may use the comment, page, and other content it has permission to access to build context. Only you can see and interact with the agent’s chat and loading states.

Work with the agent’s response

After Rovo Chat opens, the agent starts responding to your request. If the agent needs your approval before completing a task, approve the action in chat first.

When the agent has a response, it asks for your approval to leave the comment response in your thread. You can review and adjust the suggested comment before it’s added to the thread.

If you agree to share the response, the agent posts the comment directly in the thread under the original comment that mentioned it.

If you navigate away from the chat, you can return to the same conversation from the comment while the chat session is available. Read about Rovo Chat conversations and history

Comment on pages, live docs, whiteboards, blog posts, and slides

Comment on pages, live docs, whiteboards, blog posts, and slides

Comments are a great way to start a conversation about a page, live doc, or other piece of content. They allow you to remark on content, add important information, ask questions, and generally drive collaboration and teamwork by bringing others into the conversation

You can add comments in different places depending on the type of feedback you have:

  • General comments — added at the broader doc or page level, below the content of the page, live doc, or blog post you are viewing or within the comments panel; good for comments that apply to the content as a whole
  • Inline comments — added to a highlighted section of the page, doc, slide, or post you are editing or viewing; good for targeted comments on a specific word, phrase or section
Add a general comment

Comments can be added at the page, doc, or blog post level.

  • Enter your comment in the comment field at the bottom of the screen, or the bottom of the comments panel that is accessed from the floating action bar at the bottom right of your screen.
  • By default, Watch this content is selected. This means you’ll start receiving notifications about the content. Clear the checkbox if you don’t want to watch the content.
  • Select Add (Ctrl+S or ⌘+S) Other users can reply to and/or react to your comment. You or a space administrator can edit your comment(s).
Add inline comments

You can add inline comments by highlighting text or hovering over a section on a page, blog post, doc, or slide.

To add an inline comment by highlighting:

  • Highlight the text you want to comment on
  • Select Comment from the floating toolbar that appears above the highlighted text
  • Enter your comment and select Add (Ctrl+S or ⌘+S) If you add a comment while editing a page, the comment is only visible to others editing the page, and it doesn’t appear to viewers or trigger relevant notifications until the page is published.

Images can be added to inline comments, but only by those with edit access to the page.

Add inline comments to images and videos

You can add inline comments to both images and videos that you have added to your page or doc.

When editing:

  • Select the image or video

  • Select the Comment button in the toolbar

  • Enter your comment and select Add (Ctrl+S or ⌘+S) When viewing:

  • Hover over the image or video

  • Select the Comment button that appears

  • Enter your comment and select Add (Ctrl+S or ⌘+S)

Add inline comments to whiteboards

Comments are a great addition to collaboration on whiteboards. You can use comments to give feedback, ask questions, or leave notes throughout the board.

To add a comment:

  • Select Comments from the toolbar or press C to enter comment mode.
  • Select where you want to place the comment. The comment window will open.
  • Enter your comment and select Save (Ctrl+S or ⌘+S)
View inline comments

After an inline comment is added to a page or doc, the selected text will be highlighted in yellow; select any highlighted text to display the related comment(s).

If an inline comment is added to an image or a video, a small icon is shown in the top right corner of the image; select the icon to display the related comment(s).

When you and your team add comments to a whiteboard, they’re displayed on the canvas in the regions or locations they were added to. You can view and reply to them right from the canvas. You can also view and manage comments from the comment sidebar when you enter comment mode.

Just like page, doc, and blog post comments, others can reply to, or like, your inline comments, and you’ll be notified when they do.

Review all comments in a single panel

To review, triage, and interact with all comments – both inline and general – added to a page or live doc in a single panel, select Show comments from the floating action bar on the bottom right of the screen. If there are enough in-depth comments on the content, Rovo will generate a summary of unresolved general and inline comments.

To filter and sort what appears in your panel, select Filter and sort from the top right of the panel. There you can filter to show only unread comments, only resolved comments, or all open comments (including unread ones).

Comments can be sorted from top to bottom (in order that they’ve been added to the content) or newest to oldest. Lastly, you can opt to only display general comments and hide all inline comments.

Resolve inline comments

Inline comments have a time and place during the lifecycle of your content. Once the feedback has been read and implemented, keeping those highlighted sections around may no longer add value.

You can resolve an inline comment whether you are editing or viewing content to remove the highlight. The option to resolve is available when viewing the initial inline comment only; you can’t resolve a reply to an inline comment.

See all the resolved comments, filter for Resolved from the comments panel.

To reopen a resolved comment, select the green Reopen check to the right of the comment.

If an inline comment was added and resolved during a single editing session, only people who can edit the page can see the comment in the list of resolved comments. This stealthy way of commenting behind the scenes is a great way to collaborate on content without involving those with view-only access.

Rich comments

Inline and general comments might look simple, but they support rich text (like bold, underline, and italics), bulleted and numbered lists, links and anchors, and @mentions. You can also drop images into any comment to really illustrate your point.

Link to a comment

You can link directly to an inline comment or a general comment by copying the link to it.

  • Hover over the timestamp and a link icon appears.
  • Select the link to copy the comments location to your clipboard.
  • Paste that link to share that location with someone else.
Comment permissions

Administrators of a space have the option to turn off commenting entirely.

If comments are allowed in a space:

  • you can add comments in a space.
  • you can edit the comments you added.
  • you can delete your own comments, but only if there are no replies to your comment. Whether deleting your own comment or a comment from someone else, keep in mind that deleted comments can’t be restored.
Space admin controls

There is no permission that controls comments across the entire site, but space admins can:

  • edit any comments in their space. The timestamp on a comment always indicates when the comment was last edited.
  • delete any comments in their space and give other people the power to remove comments with the ‘Remove Comments’ permission.
  • prevent comments from being created in their space by removing the ‘Add Comments’ permission from the ‘confluence-users’ or ‘users’ groups, and also the anonymous users and all other users and groups. Select Watch settings from the More actions (…) menu to receive an email notification whenever anyone edits or adds a comment to content.

On blog posts only, an AUTHOR lozenge will appear on any comments made by the original author of the post.

It’s not possible to delete all comments on a page simultaneously, or change the order of comments.

Create a network of users

Create a network of users

You can create a network of users who are important to you, to make sure you’re always up to date with their Confluence activity. You might want to follow your boss or teammates, to see what they’re working on, or whoever creates the most entertaining blog posts.

When someone’s part of your network, we’ll send you a notification when they:

  • Add or edit pages, live docs, or blog posts
  • Comment on pages, live docs, and blog posts, or edit a comment
  • Update their user profile
Follow another user

You can follow (or unfollow) another user in multiple ways:

  • Access their profile card by clicking or hovering over their avatar or name and then select Follow.
  • To follow a user with their hover profile, hover your mouse over their profile picture when it appears on a page and choose Follow.
  • To follow a user from your Network view:
    • Choose your profile picture at the right side of the navigation, then choose Network
    • Search for and select the user in the User name field and click Follow
    • Reload your Network view and the profile picture of the user(s) you just followed will appear in the Following list on the right. Once you’re following a user, you’ll start seeing their activity in your Following feed on Home. This gives you a quick snapshot of the pages and projects that individual is focused on.
Access your network view

To see what’s been happening in your network, access your network view as described above.

You can access another user’s network view using the hover profile by choosing More > Network Page.

  • RSS feeds – You can subscribe to any Confluence user’s network RSS feed and get summaries on the activity of other users they’re following. See Subscribe to a network RSS feed.
  • Email notifications – You can request email notifications of any activity in your network. See Subscribe to email notifications.

Mention a person or team

Mention a person or team

Mentions (also known as @mentions) are a seamless way to draw a person’s or team’s attention to pages, live docs, comments, or a task you’ve assigned to them.

There are two ways to add mentions in Confluence Cloud:

  • using autocomplete.
  • via the editor toolbar. People who are @mentioned will receive a notification and (if they’re subscribed) an email letting them know.

An important exception: During the trial period of any Confluence Cloud plan, people who are @mentioned will receive the notification, but not the email. This is true even if the person is subscribed to email.

Once the trial has concluded, email will be added as a secondary means of informing people when they’re @mentioned.

Notifications and/or emails are sent the first time you mention people on a page, but not for subsequent mentions.

If you need to catch someone’s attention, and you’ve already mentioned them, try sharing content with them instead.

Mention a person

When you mention a person or assign a task to them, they’ll receive a notification in their notification drawer as well as an email (if they’re subscribed). Any task assigned to them will also appear under Tasks.

Use autocomplete

To mention a person using autocomplete, type ‘@’ in the editor, then start typing their name. Choose the person you want to mention from the list of suggestions.

You can use autocomplete mentions in Jira Cloud as well. To learn about using mentions and other features to collaborate on Jira issues, go to this page.

Use the editor or toolbar

If you’d rather use the toolbar or editor, type @ or choose the @ icon, then start typing the name of the person you want to mention. Choose the person you want to mention from the list of suggestions.

Assign an action to a person

You can describe an action and mention someone and they will be assigned to complete this action.

To create an action item and assign it:

  • Type []or select Action item from the toolbar.
  • Describe the action.
  • Type @ and mention someone by name. They will be notified that they have an action to complete. When they complete the action, they can return to the action item and select it to mark it complete.
Mention a team

You can also mention a team in the same way you mention a person, but only for teams with 50 members or less.

When you mention a team or assign them a task, individuals in that team will receive notifications in their notification drawer, as well as an email (if they’re subscribed). Any task assigned to them will also appear under Tasks.

Use autocomplete

To mention a team using autocomplete, type ‘@’ in the editor, then start typing the team name. Choose the team you want to mention from the list of suggestions. The suggestions will also include teams whose profile description contains the word or phrase entered.

Use the editor toolbar

If you’d rather use the editor toolbar, choose the @ icon, then start typing the name of the team you want to mention. Choose the team you want to mention from the list of suggestions. The suggestions will also include teams whose profile description contains the word or phrase entered.

Mentioning more than one agent in the same comment isn’t supported yet.

To invoke and interact with an agent in a comment, open the Confluence content you want to work on, and:

  • Start a general comment or an inline comment. Read about adding comments
  • In the comment, enter @, then start typing the name of the agent you want to invoke.
  • Choose the agent from the menu. You may see a mix of people and agents, depending on who or what you’ve recently worked with.
  • Finish typing your request as a comment, then select Add. While you’re drafting, Confluence lets you know that the agent will respond in Rovo Chat. After you publish the comment, Rovo Chat opens in the side panel with the mentioned agent selected and the conversation started.

The agent may use the comment, page, and other content it has permission to access to build context. Only you can see and interact with the agent’s chat and loading states.

Use the editor toolbar

If you’d rather use the editor toolbar, choose the @ icon, then start typing the name of the team you want to mention. Choose the team you want to mention from the list of suggestions. The suggestions will also include teams whose profile description contains the word or phrase entered.

Share Confluence content

Share Confluence content

You can use the Share window in Confluence to send people a link to your page, live doc, blog, whiteboard, database, or Smart Link in the content tree. This is a great way to invite your team to collaborate or to distribute information to large groups of people.

Share by email

Using the Share button to share content with specific people, groups, teams, or email addresses will trigger an email notification to the recipients that contains a link to the content.

Recipients will also receive a Confluence notification in the notification bell, as well as push notifications in Confluence mobile.

To share Confluence content by email:

  • Open the content item in Confluence Cloud.
  • Select the Share button in the top right.
  • Start typing the name of a person or group to see a list of suggestions, then select the right ones from the list.
    • Or you can one-click add suggested users who will appear along the bottom of the search bar.
    • Repeat this step to add multiple recipients.
    • Note: teams are not yet compatible with Share.
  • If applicable, choose whether they should be able to view or edit. (This will apply to everyone you’ve added in the search bar.)
    • Emails and teams can’t be assigned permissions, only notified.
  • Leave the notify box checked to send a notification. Uncheck it to prevent notifications from being sent.
  • (Optional) Add a custom message.
  • Select Share. Need to troubleshoot access to your content?

If you’re on the Premium or Enterprise plan, you can use the inspect permissions feature to quickly find out what’s blocking someone from accessing a content item.

For more tips, see Troubleshoot access problems to content.

Share using a link

If you don’t want to use a Confluence notification to notify people about content, or if you want to include a link to the content item in an email you create yourself, you can copy the link to the content item.

Sharing the link alone doesn’t grant access

Giving someone a link doesn’t automatically grant them access to the content. Check the content item’s access settings in Share to make sure people have the right access.

For help interpreting who has access, check out Change who can find content and what they can do with it.

To share using a link:

  • You’ll find a link icon next to the Share button. Select it to copy the link.
    • You can also just copy the content item’s URL from your browser window.
  • Paste the link into an email, Slack, or anywhere else you want to share it.
Share to Slack

Save yourself the context switching and extra clicks of sharing Confluence content in Slack by doing it directly from Confluence. You can find the Share to Slack functionality in the Share window.

The Confluence Slack app is a system app and is installed by default for all Confluence sites, so anyone can use it without needing an admin to install it.

Connect a Slack workspace

When you first use Share to Slack, you’ll be prompted to connect the Slack workspace where you want to share. Simply Sign in to enable sharing to Slack directly from Confluence. To connect an additional workspace, select Add new workspace.

Send content to Slack channels

After selecting Share to Slack for the content you want to share:

  • Choose which Slack workspace to send to.
  • Choose the channel or person in that workspace.
  • (Optional) Add a custom message.
  • Select Share.
Inviting external users

When you share content with someone outside of Confluence, we send them an email inviting them to join your site. They’ll be prompted to create an Atlassian account before they can access your content.

When you invite an external user, you grant them access to Confluence, not just to your specifically shared content. We add them to the default product group and start billing you for the new user.

In some cases, your invitation will be sent to an admin for approval first. This happens when:

  • Your site doesn’t allow existing users to invite others to join.
  • The recipient’s email address domain, like @gmail.com, isn’t on your site’s list of approved domains. If an admin declines your request, you’ll be notified by email. The external recipient won’t be notified.

Want to share a content item externally to anyone on the internet?

If public links public links are allowed on your site, you can share individual content items publicly with anyone on the internet.

Share content externally with public links

Share content externally with public links

Public links allow teams to share individual Confluence content items with people outside of Confluence without giving them access to Confluence. This could be useful for sharing information to the public, like customer FAQs, release notes, shareholder letters, and more.

On this page, you’ll find guidance on how to use public links to share your content with anyone on the internet.

For details on how public links work, go to How secure are public links?

If you’re an admin looking for guidance on how to get started with public links, go to Control whether spaces can allow public links.

Public links are only available on Confluence’s paid plans (Standard, Premium, and Enterprise). Only Confluence pages, live docs, and whiteboards can have public links, not any other type of Confluence content (e.g., blogs, databases, etc.).

Turn on a public link

A public link is available for any page, live doc, and whiteboard in Confluence (your admin allows them). Always use caution when sharing content externally.

Content items will only ever have one public link

If you turn a public link off, anyone who already has it won’t be able to access the content anymore. But if you later turn the public link back on, those people will again be able to access the content because it’s the same link.

To turn on and share a public link:

  • Go to the content item you want a public link for.

  • Open Share in the top right.

  • Turn on the public link toggle at the bottom of the window.

  • The public link will be automatically copied, for your convenience.

  • Or if the public link toggle is already on, select Copy public link.

  • Paste the link in an email, a chat tool, on social media — wherever you want to communicate with the audience for the content. If you can’t turn on a public link, then you don’t have permission to turn it on. This could be because:

  • public links aren’t allowed in the space (or on your site)

  • the specific public link has been blocked by an admin

  • you don’t have permission to edit the content item

  • you don’t have space permission to edit restrictions for content in the space Be aware that anyone you share a public link with can share that link with anyone they want to. As long as the public toggle is on, anyone on the internet with the public link can view the content, whether you shared directly with them or not.

Also, be aware that anyone who can view your internal content item can copy its public link and share it with anyone on the internet.

Make sure to share the correct link

You need the actual public link from the Share window or else anyone on the internet you share with won’t be able to view the content. The link in your browser is not the public link.

To view what public link visitors see:

  • Copy the public link.
  • Open a new tab in your browser.
  • Paste the public link in the new tab. Or you can copy the public link, log out of your Atlassian account, and paste the public link in any browser tab.

Note: Custom emojis will display on public content by default. If you want to prevent this and you’re an organization admin, you can go to Atlassian Administration > Site settings > Emoji and turn the toggle off for Allow custom emojis on publicly shared content. If custom emojis aren’t allowed on public content, they’ll display as text — their custom emoji name framed with two colons, such as :dancingbird:

To turn off a public link:

  • Go to the content item you want a public link for.
  • Open Share in the top right.
  • Turn off the public link toggle at the bottom of the window. Anyone on the internet who still has the public link is blocked from viewing the content as long as the public link toggle is off.
What to know when sharing public links

Always use caution when sharing content externally. Here are a few key points to know for using public links safely.

Internal view restrictions don’t apply

As long as your admins allow you to use public links, a public link will just work, regardless of any view restrictions. Public links ignore any restrictions to who can access a parent item, the space, and the site itself.

No matter who is restricted from viewing the internal content item, anyone on the internet who you share the public link with will be able to view its content.

Public links hide sensitive information

Visitors will see a safe, view-only version of the content that hides any content outside of the shared content (content tree, macros, etc.) and locks most Confluence functionality.

To learn more about what public link visitors can see, go to the “What is hidden from visitors” section of How secure are public links?

Public links don’t share branches of the content tree

Each public link corresponds to one content item only. If you turn on and share a public link for a content item that has any child items, the public link will only reveal the parent item, not any of the child items. To share the child items too, you’ll need to turn on their public links and share each of them individually.

What to expect from public whiteboards

Public whiteboards differ from public pages in that, firstly, whiteboard visitors can edit the whiteboard if the whiteboard’s public link has been set to Can edit.

Secondly, whiteboards differ from pages in that they are live, in real-time; changes to them don’t need to be published before visitors can see them.

This makes public whiteboards useful for sharing roadmaps, brainstorms, holding workshops, and more.

Visitors are represented in the top toolbar and as a cursor moving across the whiteboard while they’re viewing and/or editing it. They can see collaborators working on the board and other anonymous visitors.

Anyone visiting the public whiteboard will be represented as “Anonymous”, even if they can access the internal whiteboard link.

Collaborators can see anonymous visitors and their cursors from the internal version of the whiteboard and can control what name appears under their cursor to anonymous visitors.

Anonymous users will be able to view your public name. To update how your name appears to anonymous users:

  • Select your avatar, then Manage Account.
  • In the Profile and visibility tab, select your name under Public name.
  • Enter how you would like your name to appear publicly, then save. Your changes will take effect within five minutes.
